bib.title: InfCode: Adversarial Iterative Refinement of Tests and Patches for Reliable Software Issue Resolution

legacy_report:
SOURCE: InfCode: Adversarial Iterative Refinement of Tests and Patches for Reliable Software Issue Resolution. Kefan Li (first author) et al., Beihang University and Beijing Tokfinity. Preprint (arXiv 2511.16004v1, cs.SE), November 2025 (arXiv date 20 Nov 2025; ACM-format template, not a published venue).
COVERAGE: 13 of 13 pages read; extraction was 44,171 chars. I read the text through the conclusion and the start of the reference list (about 34,500 chars) and skipped the remaining references. There are no appendices. Extraction was clean. Figure 2's Venn labels are garbled text, so I did not use them.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- Claim: A test generator and a code generator iterate adversarially. When the code passes, the test agent adds harder tests, and the loop stops at a hard iteration cap or as soon as strengthened tests still pass. This makes the scorekeeper itself something the loop improves.
  number: none
  setup: Stage 1 of InfCode, inside a per-issue Docker container.
  quote: "To prevent unbounded iteration between the Test Generator and the Code Generator, we impose a hard cap on the number of iterations, once this limit is reached, the generation process terminates immediately. In addition, if the Test Generator strengthens the test suite and the code still passes all tests, the refinement loop terminates at once."
  where: p.4, Sec 2.2
- Claim: On SWE-bench Verified with Claude 4.5 Sonnet, InfCode reports 79.4% (397), rank 1, ahead of TRAE + Doubao-Seed-Code at 78.80%.
  number: 79.4% (397 issues)
  setup: SWE-bench Verified leaderboard as of 14 Nov 2025. Only the top five other entries are compared. Only the method and backbone model are named. No cost, run count or seed information is given.
  quote: "🏆InfCode 79.4% (397) 1" and "TRAE + Doubao-Seed-Code 78.80% (394) 2"
  where: p.7, Table 3
- Claim: Ablation on SWE-bench Lite shows both parts help, and selection matters more than the adversarial loop. Removing adversarial iteration costs 4 points. Removing selection costs 8 points.
  number: 40.33% (121) full; 36.33% (109) w/o Adversarial; 32.33% (97) w/o Selection
  setup: SWE-bench Lite (300 issues), DeepSeek-V3, a single configuration per row. No variance is reported.
  quote: "InfCode 40.33% (121) w/o Adversarial 36.33% (109) w/o Selection 32.33% (97)"
  where: p.7, Table 2
- Claim: On SWE-bench Lite with DeepSeek-V3, InfCode beats the baselines at modest cost.
  number: 40.33% (121), $0.26 per issue. KGCompass: 36.67% (110), $0.20. Agentless with GPT-4o: 32.00%, $0.70.
  setup: SWE-bench Lite, 300 issues. Baseline numbers come from their own papers and the leaderboard, so they are not rerun. Backbone models differ across rows.
  quote: "KGCompass [24] DeepSeek-V3 36.67% (110) 0.20 InfCode DeepSeek-V3 40.33% (121)0.26"
  where: p.6, Table 1
- Claim: A Selector agent reads all candidate patches and their test patches, can run them in the container, and filters out overfitted or unstable ones. It is an agent-as-judge that backs the tests with execution.
  number: none
  setup: Stage 2. The selection criteria are named only in general terms (functional correctness, coverage, execution success, repo compatibility). No prompt or scoring formula is given.
  quote: "It then compares their performance, filtering out overfitted or unstable solutions."
  where: p.4, Sec 2.3
- Claim: Authors concede the adversarial test generator can drift from the issue and mislead the code generator. This is a reward-hacking-style failure of the scorekeeper.
  number: none
  setup: Observed in log analysis. It is not quantified.
  quote: "during adversarial iterations, the Test Generator sometimes creates specialized tests that deviate from the issue description in order to induce failures, which in turn misleads the Code Generator."
  where: p.8, Sec 6
- Claim: Guard against the agent weakening its own checker. Files beginning with "test" are excluded from the evaluated diff.
  number: none
  setup: Evaluation uses official SWE-bench CLI after git diff extraction.
  quote: "we excluded all files starting with test from the evaluation."
  where: p.5, Sec 3.3. See also p.9, internal validity.
- Claim: Tool usage per solved problem: Bash is about 302.6 calls (61.0%), Editor 167.01 (33.6%), Searcher 22.06 (4.4%), Submitter 4.74 (1.0%). Bash fails 10.04% of the time and Editor 5.80%.
  number: see claim
  setup: Averages per problem. Model and dataset for this measurement are not stated.
  quote: "Searcher (22.06) Submitter (4.74) Bash T ool (302.6) Editor (167.01)"
  where: p.8, Fig 3

LIMITS
- Authors concede test-generator drift and tool failures (p.8). The paper itself flags that Lite may have "insufficient test intensity".
- No ablation of test quality itself, for example how often generated tests are wrong. No cost or iteration-cap value is given. The cap is never stated numerically.
- Baselines are copied from other papers or the leaderboard, with mixed backbones. There is one run per cell and no confidence intervals.
- The Selector's criteria are only loosely described.
- The Construct Validity section claims "cross-validation against multiple independent test generations", but no such experiment appears in the results.
- The 79.4% leaderboard claim has probably been overtaken by now (today is 2026-11-06).
- Language generality is asserted, not tested. Only Python SWE-bench was evaluated.

INTERNAL INCONSISTENCY
- The text says "InfCode with Deepseek-V3 ... successfully solves 118 problems". Table 1, Table 2 and the abstract-level claims say 121 (40.33%). Cite the table figure, 121, and flag the 118.
- The text also says InfCode "solved 11 more problems than KGCompass". The table gap is 121 - 110 = 11, which matches the table, not 118.

BUILDS ON
- Test-and-patch co-generation: LLM-LOOP [35], CoCoEvo [19].
- Verification in the loop: LEVER [29].
- Execution-feedback and self-correction work: self-debugging (Chen et al. [10]), Self-Refine [26], Reflexion [37], RLEF [14].
- Self-debugging with self-generated tests [11], RepairAgent [6].
- Issue-reproduction tests: Otter (Ahmed et al. 2025) and TDD-Bench Verified (Ahmed et al. 2024). The paper cites these as showing agents can write wrong tests.
- Agent scaffolds and pipelines: SWE-agent [44], OpenHands [40], Agentless [42], Trae Agent [13].
- Benchmarks: SWE-bench [16], SWE-bench Verified [33].
- Bracketed numbers are the paper's reference indices. Author-year pairs are given only where the printed reference list showed them.

CODE: none.

FIGURES
- Fig 1 (p.3): Overview of InfCode. Issue plus container feed a Test Generator and a Code Generator in an adversarial loop. Each emits a git-diff patch. A Selector runs the candidates in the container and picks one. It shows the two-stage shape of generate then select, with the scorekeeper as an evolving component. Good deck candidate.
- Fig 3 (p.8): Tool-call distribution and failure rates. It is secondary and only weakly relevant.
- Fig 2 (p.6): Venn overlap of resolved issues. Low value.

FIT TO NOTE
- 03-the-scorekeeper.md fits well for these points: weak tests let patches pass wrongly; a test-writing agent can raise the bar; the Selector is a judge that executes candidates; the hard iteration cap and early-stop rule; the guard against editing test files; and the test-drift limitation (the scorekeeper can itself be gamed).
- 08-self-improving-loops.md could take the adversarial co-evolution angle as a secondary cite.
- 09-failure-modes-and-guardrails.md could take the test-drift and test-file-exclusion points.
- Verdict: 03 is the best primary fit.

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions found. The 118 vs 121 inconsistency is flagged above. Fig 2 text is garbled. The ACM DOI is a template placeholder.
